problem.para: In the body of the Working Draft, there occasionally appears a point that requires particular attention, highlighted thus:
Text of the problem.

It is a language opportunity to provide an annex, probably informative, that defines host language bindings that realize the abstract API defined in this document for at least one widely used programming language Java, C++, or Python). This should include calling GQL procedures from the host language and calling functions and/or procedures, which are written in this or another host language, from within GQL.
Doing so will validate that the specification of the abstract API is complete and sufficiently well-defined to enable language bindings to be defined.

LO.brief: Concept of deterministic predicates and expressions

problem.comment: Editorial: Stefan Plantikow 2021-04-26 Converted to LO
problem.para: SQL pays a lot of attention as to whether an expression is deterministic or not, as this has consequences for its use in constraints. If GQL is to have a schema for graphs that includes constraints, then this will also need considerable attention.
Consider explicit support for additional collations other than UCS_BASIC and UNICODE ( case insensitive variants, use of alternative collation tables).
Aggregation would benefit from being improved for the needs of GQL:

ulist.item: Revisit the set of provided aggregation functions in light of existing products and market needs ( add TIMES or graph-specific aggregation functions).

Provide means to better control how aggregation functions behave on empty inputs (no rows), by allowing the user to specify a default value or default failure behavior for aggregation on empty inputs.

Allow aggregation to scope over whole subqueries (partition by), possibly taking advantage of using fixed variables as implicit grouping keys and supporting the evaluation of aggregation functions over the incoming working table in every statement.

problem.para: See also .

LO.brief: Define path pattern union using left recursion

problem.para: Path pattern union is not defined using left recursion. SXM-052 believed that it should be possible to support left recursion but declined to do so for expediency. It is a Language Opportunity to support left recursion.
Linked to .

Currently transaction demarcation is defined such that any failure within a GQL-request procedure will cause a rollback attempt. Rollback on failure may not be the best option here. Consider an application that has multiple procedure invocations within a transaction context where the first N procedures succeed but procedure n+1 fails. It would be preferable to decide in the application logic whether to commit or rollback, by using a session level configuration mechanism or by providing options to transaction demarcation commands.

SQL, Cypher, and possibly other property graph query languages have various styles of regular expression substring functions as well as other possibly relevant string value functions that GQL currently is missing. It is a Language Opportunity to add functionality equivalent to at least that of SQL to GQL.

problem.para: It has been proposed that a macro name may be a in a .
Linked to .

LO.brief: TTL and auto-delete of graph elements

problem.para: Discussion paper WG3:MMX-047 suggests the addition of a Time To Live option, which would require specified graph elements be deleted after a certain time to save storage space.
It may be possible to permit nested quantifiers. WG3:W01-014 contained a discussion of a way to support aggregates at different depths of aggregation if there are nested quantifiers.
Linked to .

It may be possible to enforce implicit joins of unconditional singletons exposed by a as part of the GRs for . This was discussed in a SQL/PG ad hoc meeting on September 8, 2020. It was decided not to attempt that change as part of WG3:W04-009R1, leaving it as a future possibility.
Linked to .
The ability to specify cheapest queries (analogous to SHORTEST but minimizing the sum of costs along a path) is desirable.
Linked to .

In addition to SHORTEST GROUP, it has been proposed to support SHORTEST [ k ] WITH TIES, with the semantics to return the first k matches (where k defaults to 1) when sorting matches in ascending order on number of edges, and also return any matches that have the same number of edges as the last of the k matches. This is the semantics of WITH TIES in in SQL/Foundation.
Linked to .
WG3:W04-009R1 believed it should be possible to support nested selectors using recursion but did not undertake that. It is a Language Opportunity to support nested selectors.
Linked to .

problem.para: WG3:W04-009R1 believed it should be possible to support selectors within quantifiers with a finite upper bound, but did not undertake that. It is a Language Opportunity to support selectors within quantifiers with a finite upper bound.

Support for grouped procedure calls needs to be specified. A grouped procedure call invokes a procedure for each partition of the binding table and combines (concatenates) all results received. Partitions may be determined by a user-specified grouping key or perhaps sets of grouping keys.
See also .

LO.brief: Additional synonyms for undirected edge patterns

problem.para: In the BNF for , the delimiter tokens <~[ ]~> have been suggested as a synonym for -[ ]- as part of . The synonym for the - () would then be <~>, the synonym for would use the delimiter tokens <~/ /~> and the synonym for would use the tokens <~ and > surrounding a label as originally proposed in WG3:MMX-060. These synonyms might be considered to make the table of edge patterns more harmonious and internally consistent.
Linked to .
SQL/Foundation defines five operators that use XQuery regular expression syntax:
These REGEX operators could be very useful and should be considered.

LO.brief: IEEE 754 floating point literals for Infinity and NaN

problem.para: Support for approximate numeric types that are compatible with the arithmetic formats for which ISO/IEC 60559:2020/IEEE 754:2019 defines interchange formats should be added. This needs to include provisions for infinity values and literals, NaN values and literals, rounding, casting, error handling, data types, the modification of existing operations, and related conformance features.

solution.para: None provided but see paper WG3:W11-015 for a discussion.

LO.brief: Reconsider allowed behavior on loss of non-zero bytes due to truncation

problem.para: In SQL, it is whether the loss of non-zero bytes due to truncation raises an exception or not. This should be reconsidered by GQL.
Many programming languages support converting boolean types to numerics where True converts to 1 (one) and False converts to 0 (zero). Such conversions could be useful to GQL users.
Many databases and programming languages include individual type conversion functions such as:

ulist.item: toBoolean
toInteger
toFloat
toString

problem.para: If there is a need at some point to add individual conversion functions to GQL, they could be specified as syntactic transformations to the appropriate CAST function.

LO.brief: Temporal CAST with explicit FORMAT option

problem.para: In , includes an optional FORMAT that allows a user to provide a format when converting a datetime to a character string. A similar capability could be useful in GQL.
In a CAST expression, it could be useful to specify what the result should be if the CAST would otherwise raise an exception. For example:
problem.code: CAST (abc AS INT ON EXCEPTION NULL)
CAST (a.prop1 AS INT ON EXCEPTION a.prop2)
problem.para: An ON EXCEPTION capability would be particularly useful when loading large volumes of data.

LO.brief: Cast between byte strings and character strings

problem.para: does not currently support converting byte strings to character strings or character strings to byte strings (using some well-known encoding). Such a capability might be useful.

The ability to extract individual time scale components from temporal instances and duration would be useful and might be used to simplify the specification of . SQL has an EXTRACT function that satisfies a similar need and openCypher in its CIP2015-08-06 Date and Time specification has defined the ability to extract all individual time scale components.

only allows dropping a schema if it does not contain any catalog object. More user convenience could potentially be added to the by including a new option for cascading drop statements or by developing a general invalidation model for catalog objects.
Pattern Macros could provide powerful capabilities for GQL Users by providing a multi-use template. A Pattern Macro could be created in several places:

ulist.item: As a preamble to a single query that lasts for the life of the query.
As a catalog object that can be created, used in multiple queries, and lasts until explicitly dropped.

problem.para: This capability should be considered for a future GQL version.

LO.brief: Alternative syntax for testing source and destination

problem.para: The is expressed as a predicate about the node, while it is most often used to pose questions about the edge. If an alternative form of these predicates was available that put the edge as the first operand, this predicate would be more useful in combination with .
Linked to .

The bindings of a group reference flatten nested lists. This may be acceptable for SQL aggregates, which have no support for nested groupings, but may be inadequate to fully capture the semantics of a group reference in a graph pattern. MMX-035r2 section 4.1 Desynchronized lists pointed out a problem with reducing group variables to lists: two lists may be interleaved, but the reduction to separate lists can lose this information. The example given is
A solution may find matches to A and B in any order. With separate lists of matches of A and B, it will not be easy to reconstruct the precise sequence of interleaved matches to A and B.
A similar problem can arise with nested quantifiers. MMX-035r2 section 4.2 Nested quantifiers gives this example:

With this pattern, there can be 0 or more bindings to B between any two consecutive bindings to C1 and C2. With just independent lists of matches to C1, B and C2, it will not be easy to determine which bindings to B lie between which bindings to C1 and C2.
Linked to .

LO.brief: Composite queries ( set operations) on graphs

problem.para: , General Rules are written to compose the binding tables generated by pairs of queries. There might be a benefit in expanding the GRs to also support operations directly on graphs such that GQL gains the capability to do, union of graphs.
The ability to create, reference, and drop constants as catalog objects could be very useful when constructing GQL queries. This capability should be considered for a future GQL version.
The ability to query a catalog to identify graphs with particular characteristics would be useful.

Several future extensions of the GQL language (See , , ) depend on properties being directly referenceable as graph elements in their own rights. Currently properties only exist (from a schema point of view) as members in property type sets attached to either nodes or edges. A definition point of a property type as such is needed. Such a graph element will be necessary for future concept relationships between properties and, other properties, other edges and other nodes than the ones that the current property set belongs to.

LO.brief: First class properties to reify keys with functional dependencies

problem.para: Functional dependencies in a more specific manner (minimizing the need for inferencing in query planning) require explicit concept relationships between properties ( keys and non-keys) for dealing with uniqueness and key formation. See .

LO.brief: First class properties to reify versioning and timeline information

problem.para: Versioning (of both data and metadata) and timeline handling require explicit concept relationships between properties ( keys and non-keys) for dealing with uniqueness and key formation. See .

LO.brief: First class properties to map between RDF and LPG

problem.para: Coexistence between LPG(s) of different breeds and also RDF require meta transformations between concept systems describing: a source graph type, a universal abstract graph type system and a target graph type. This requires GQL properties to be directly referenceable as such in combinations with other graph elements, including other properties, edges and relationships. See .
Allowing the bundling of multiple requests into one is useful for reducing network round trips. This should include the capability for returning multiple results to the client in one round trip.

solution.para: One possibility is to introduce a new top-level Subclause <GQL-multi-request> next to .

problem.para: The ability to create and drop named stored procedures is a powerful capability when building applications in a GQL database. This capability should be considered for a future GQL version and should include both mandatory and optional parameters.

The last Informal Working Draft that contained a sketch of the functionality (deleted by W20-012) was 39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02, which is available here: https://sd.iso.org/documents/ui/#!/browse/iso/iso-iec-jtc-1/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32-wg-3/library/6/16656391_LL/16656048_LL/39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02.pdf
The ability to create, invoke, and drop named, stored queries is a powerful capability when building applications in a GQL database. This capability should be considered for a future GQL version.

The last Informal Working Draft that contained a sketch of the functionality (deleted by W20-012) was 39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02, which is available here: https://sd.iso.org/documents/ui/#!/browse/iso/iso-iec-jtc-1/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32-wg-3/library/6/16656391_LL/16656048_LL/39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02.pdf

The ability to create, call, and drop named, stored functions is a powerful capability when building applications in a GQL database. This capability should be considered for a future GQL version and should include both mandatory and optional parameters. As part of the consideration, there should be a discussion of whether GQL should support the definition and/or calling of pure functions, impure functions, or both.

The last Informal Working Draft that contained a sketch of the functionality (deleted by W20-013) was 39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02, which is available here: https://sd.iso.org/documents/ui/#!/browse/iso/iso-iec-jtc-1/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32/iso-iec-jtc-1-sc-32-wg-3/library/6/16656391_LL/16656048_LL/39075_1IWD21-GQL_2022-02.pdf
GQL should be extended to support subgraphs for the most needed use cases.
Paper WG3:RKE-046 Subgraphs of property graphs provides some commentary on this topic.
It is a Language Opportunity to support references to subpath variables, for example, in , or a TOTAL_COST function once CHEAPEST is defined.
Linked to .
There is the opportunity to support the IEEE rounding modes.
SQL/PGQ has an IS BOUND predicate to test whether an element variable is bound (See WG3:W18-028). This predicate should be considered for GQL as an advanced conformance feature.
An ordered set collection type that provides an ordered collection of distinguishable elements might be useful for GQL users.
Support for additional syntactic forms currently ruled out for should be considered.
The ability to MERGE an into an existing graph would be useful to GQL users.
See WG3:BER-089, Thoughts about MERGE, for a discussion of this topic.

GQL DROP statements should be extended to support <drop behavior> CASCADE and RESTRICT, with RESTRICT specified as the default behavior and CASCADE specified as an optional advanced conformance feature.

LO.brief: Syntax support for working with and managing persistent binding tables

problem.para: It might be useful to allow the user to store a binding table as the result of a query, rather than necessarily transmitting the final binding table to the client.

A stored binding table might subsequently be referenced as the original binding table of another procedure (instead of starting from just the unit binding table). Storing objects or references to objects might be prohibited, a stored binding table might only be supported with columns of scalar data types.

Alist.item:
GQL is a graph query language. If users would like to work with the persisted tables, they are recommended to use a system that supports SQL. Implementations that support GQL and SQL can use procedures to facilitate the use case of loading a persisted table at the beginning GQL query as the working table as illustrated by the following example:
CALL readTable(foo) YIELD a,b,c MATCH (n) WHERE n.x > c
Likewise they can facilitate the use case of persisting a GQL result by calling a GQL procedure from SQL even inline as illustrated by the following example:
CREATE TABLE foo (a,b,c) AS ( USE myGraph MATCH (n)-[k:KNOWNS]->(m) RETURN n.name AS a, m.name AS b, k.since AS c ) WITH DATA

If GQL would want to pick specifying persisted tables itself, loading a persisted table as working table could be achieved, with a FROM clause similar to the GQLs :
FROM foo MATCH (n) WHERE n.x > c
For persisting, GQL would require something akin to SQLs CREATE TABLE AS, for instance:
CREATE BINDING TABLE foo AS { USE myGraph MATCH (n)-[k:KNOWNS]->(m) RETURN n.name AS a, m.name AS b, k.since AS c }

problem.para: It could be very useful to have a mechanism for inserting a library of procedures, in a GQL schema, along with the ability to reference and execute objects in the library.
The ability to delete a path should be considered.
WG3:W22-042 said that given the lack of consensus on the mental model of the ability to delete a path removed this ability. It went on to say that:
We can illustrate how this would work with an example. Consider the following current working graph:
To delete all of the graph elements we could execute the following query:
According to the original definition, the same effect would be achievable with a path variable bound to a path of those same three elements:

As a path is a sequence of graph elements, the mental model this feature is assuming is that an instruction to delete a path is equivalent to an instruction to delete its constituent elements. A problem with this assumed mental model, however, is that unlike graph elements a path is not a persisted object. Discussions have shown a lack of consensus on treating the deletion of a path in this way. For the user attempting to delete the constituent elements of a path, an alternative would be to acquire a reference to each element and then pass them directly to the . This is not feasible, however, with variable-length paths. In the future, value functions that return lists of nodes and edges for a given path may be introduced. In that case, as an example, the following query:
would be re-writeable as:
problem.code: MATCH p = (:A)-[:S]->+(:A) FOR e IN edges(p) DELETE e FOR n IN nodes(p) DELETE n
problem.para: where edges and nodes are value functions returning from a path a list of edges and nodes respectively.
The ability to specify named parameters in addition to sequentially ordered parameters should be considered in future GQL versions.
The ability to omit intermediate optional parameters should be considered in future GQL versions. That is the optionality should not be restricted to trailing optional parameters.

LO.brief: Specify and query metadata of graphs and graph types

problem.para: It could be very useful to be able to specify and query metadata for graphs and graph types. One way to accomplish this is to have graph labels and properties that are specified when the graph and/or graph type is created. The graph properties could be accessed through a graph.graphProperty syntax. Graph labels would require a label exists function. Graph properties could be used for information such as graph creation time, a description of the graph,

It is potentially beneficial to be able to create a Graph Type with no nodes or edges and then incrementally expand the Graph Type definition using an ALTER GRAPH TYPE statement. It would also be useful to allow CREATE GRAPH with an inline to be created with an empty and incrementally enhanced with ALTER GRAPH statements. It might also be useful to have explicit syntax such as EMPTY GRAPH TYPE to allow the creation of an empty graph type for when a graph is created.

LO.brief: Remove distinction between schema and directory

problem.para: The distinction between schema and directory seems unnecessary, or at least somewhat confusing. For instance, since path traversal starts at the current schema rather than some notion of current directory, all relative paths must start with ../ to move from the current schema to its containing directory. Could not all be schemas, where one schema can contain other schemas? This should allow lifting existing syntax restrictions for the schema reference syntax and reduce the number of concepts required for the GQL-catalog.

Some care would be needed to make it clear that a schema S contained in schema PARENT is an independent schema, not an extension of PARENT. GQL does not currently implement directory or schema access controls; if and when it does, and if this LO is implemented, the notion of a schema TRAVERSAL access right (as opposed to a schema READ access right) might be useful.

LO.brief: Parameter support in CREATE and DROP

problem.para: The create and drop schema, graph, and graph type statements might benefit from allowing to specify the schema, graph, or graph type to be created or dropped.
It is a language opportunity to provide either a normative specification of a graph serialization format or to provide guidance on graph serialization in a guidance standard.

LO.brief: Defaults for implementation-provided transaction access modes

problem.para: It is a language opportunity to provide some standard specifications for modeled on the existing SQL specifications. However, it should also recognize that since the time the SQL specifications were made there are more recently-defined levels such as Snapshot Isolation or Serializable Snapshot Isolation, or other industrially-applied or theoretical variants.

Some applications (such as recommender systems) require queries involving nodes with unique IDs and expect the match statement to always return something to be processed for other queries. Consider additional syntax to handle non-matched patterns and provide the user with a powerful facility to detect semantic errors and failing early in the case of errors, thus avoiding unnecessary work and providing good diagnostics regarding which pattern failed to match.

LO.brief: Allow unions between node types in edge type definitions

problem.para: It could be useful to allow endpoint definitions in an edge type definition to be patterns that potentially match multiple node type definitions within the graph type.

LO.brief: Allow use of element type names in value types

problem.para: It could be useful to allow s and s to resolve to existing node types and edge types using node type names and edge type names. Such a capability would need to identify a graph type where the node types and edge types might be found, either through the graph type of the current working graph or through identifying a schema and graph type.

LO.brief: Disallow distinct node and edge types with the same name

problem.para: It could be useful to restrict node type names and edge type names to be in the same namespace. That is, node type names are unique in the set of node type and edge type names in a graph type, and edge type names unique in the set of node type and edge type names in a graph type.

It could be useful to have functions that return the number of edges pointing into a node (INDEGREE) and the number of edges pointing out from a node (OUTDEGREE). Such functions should take into account undirected edges.

LO.brief: Comparison predicates with more than two argument expressions

problem.para: Comparison predicate rules could be extended in the future to support comparing more than two value expressions at the same time. For instance, how would GQL handle the evaluation of 2<3<1.

LO.brief: Returning multiple outcomes when executing multiple requests

problem.para: WG3:W24-009 P00-WG3-077 suggests that it would be useful to allow the bundling of multiple requests into one as a way of reducing network round trips. This should include the capability for returning multiple results to the client in one round trip. One possibility is to introduce a new top-level Subclause <GQL-multi-request> next to .

WG3:W24-009 P00-WG3-102 suggests that according to the Working Drafts philosophy of equally supporting an SQL-flavored syntax for easier onboarding of SQL developers, it would be beneficial to add data modification statements that are SQL-inspired.

solution.para: Adding syntax that supports, for example:
solution.code: DELETE v FROM personGraph MATCH (p:Person)-[v:VOTED_FOR]->(:Person) WHERE p.age < 18
UPDATE p SET p.teen = TRUE FROM personGraph MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.age < 18
solution.para: Both examples reuse the FROM clause of the .

LO.brief: Testing whether conditional variables are bound

problem.para: GQL could benefit from a predicate checking if a conditional variable is bound. One can check it with what is already there, for example, if an element x has property a, one can check (x.a=x.a) IS NOT NULL, but this is not a very natural way. This could be useful in patterns such as [ (A)? -> [ (B) -> (C) WHERE A.X = B.X+C.X ] -> (D)]{2}. In such patterns that appear to be allowed (see also comment WG3:W24-009 P00-WG3-144) one may want to test in the WHERE clause whether A is bound.

LO.brief: ALTER GRAPH TYPE and ALTER GRAPH

problem.para: Support for ALTER GRAPH TYPE and ALTER GRAPH statements should be considered.
Consider, in future versions of GQL, looking at the possibility of using multiple s in a while providing more advanced capabilities, such as handling list of lists or record types within the .
SQL/Foundation defines <array element reference> to return the i-th element of an array. A similar way of referencing the i-th element of a list should be considered.
SQL/Foundation defines GREATEST and LEAST operators. It needs to be decided if these additional operators should be included.
Syntax rules determining the declared type of sites should be revisited to improve and specify (where lacking) the inference of the nullability of those sites.

The document relies on immediate containment to a great extent. Experience in SQL suggests that immediate containment is very fragile and therefore to be avoided if possible. The document should be swept for instances of immediate containment that could be replaced by some more robust form of containment.

LO.brief: Add more pretty figures and diagrams

problem.para: The document could benefit from some additional diagrams to clarify aspects of the specification.
The following aspects have been suggested:

olist.item: There are a lot of things in GQL that could be considered some form of executable (programs, requests, commands, procedures, function, statements, query, and others). The document needs a hierarchical diagram laying out the hierarchy of those to make the concepts accessible to the reader.

The current execution context, the current request context, and the current session context seem to form some kind of hierarchy. It might be nice to have a diagram showing the nesting of these contexts.

LO.brief: Relax syntax constraints on value queries

problem.para: The Syntax Rules of could be made more permissive with regard to the contained to allow for more subqueries that syntactically guarantee to return a binding table with one column and at most one record. Paper WG3:UTC-064 has a discussion of cases not covered in Syntax Rules introduced by this paper.
It would be appropriate to consider <distinct predicate> in future versions of GQL.

LO.brief: GR classification by possible kinds of side effects

problem.para: Resolution of WG3:CMN-019 P00-USA-351 and P00-USA-353 has removed remaining uses of active voice in General Rules. While alignment with WG3:SD-004 is appropriate, these changes also removed the use of active voice as a mechanism for indicating which General Rules modify the GQL-environment, GQL-data, or any of the major kinds of contexts, which General Rules perform side-effects. However, being able to easily identify such General Rules seems desirable for the reader.

solution.para: Develop a facility for the further (informative) classification of General rules as catalog-modifying, data-modifying,
Classifications should be indicated on the rules ( by an informative note or some kind of tag such as [DATA CHANGE]) as well as in an informative annex listing all rules with the same classification.
Expansion of this facility to certain kinds of SRs (type inference, type requirement, rewrite, ) and CRs (removal of surface syntax) could be considered.

problem.para: By default, the trim functions (TRIM, BTRIM, LTRIM, and RTRIM) remove leading and trailing space characters. When data might be copied and pasted, it is easy for a user to include whitespace characters other than spaces. While it is possible to specify a trim string that contains all whitespace characters, it is tedious to do so. It would be useful to include support for trimming whitespace in GQL.

From GQL DIS comment P00-NLD-044, ANTLR4 is a well-known parser generator and there is already known interest in an ANTLR4 version of the GQL syntax. (See https://github.com/TuGraph-family/gql-grammar).
An ANTLR4 version of the GQL syntax should be developed and possibly replace the existing gql-standard.bnf.txt artifact.

LO.brief: Consider removal of aliasing BNF non-terminal definitions

problem.para: From GQL DIS comment P00-USA-362, Is any purpose served by a subclause whose only BNF is:

Can we simplify by just deleting one of these two BNF non-terminals? Note that the SRs and GRs do not add value, they merely pass along the static and the dynamic information from one BNF non-terminal to the other. LO.brief: Nested transactions and step-wise request execution and rollback

PP.brief: Ensure type lattice of each base type can be closed by union types

problem.para: All value types defined by the standard form a lattice with uniquely defined upper and lower bounds for any finite set of value types as well both a top (ANY) and a bottom (NOTHING) type. However, some of the data types inherited from do not guarantee the existence of upper bounds among the types of the same static base type.

As a consequence of this, static value type combination is currently forced to pick some arbitrary type that is not a proper upper bound for certain inputs. Further, this design prevents implementations with support for dynamic union types to naturally close per-base type sublattices by generating an appropriate dynamic union type via general value type combination.

This unnecessarily complicates and restricts implementations interested in providing dynamic union type support. A possible solution would be to allow implementations to fail in static value type combination where no common upper bound exists for the given inputs in a respective static base type. This relaxation of the current regime would then enable general value type combination to close the lattice by producing the closed dynamic union type of the inputs.
This issue in a narrow sense needs to be solved for numeric types.

More broadly, for certain kinds of types, the current rules of static value type combination are unnecessarily broad, forcing the return of base type-specific supertypes where a more specific union type would be available in certain implementations. This should be reviewed regarding whether the return of union types could be considered permissible, too. From a quick look at , this secondary issue seems to apply to: byte string types, character string types, the zoned-ness of temporal instant types, and reference value types.
Both suggested solutions would be backward-compatible.

Certain data-modifying statements (SET, REMOVE, ) need to resolve conflicting updates caused by processing the rows of the incoming working table. Currently, conflict resolution of this nature is specified somewhat ad-hoc in the General Rules of each statement in a way that gives a lot of freedom to implementations but does not provide deterministic outcomes, hampering portability of queries. Applying generally agreed principles of substitution in object-oriented languages, a subclass MySubEdgeTypeFamily <: MyEdgeTypeFamily that wants to override endpoints could narrow its type to any subtype of endpoints in MyEdgeTypeFamily, such as (A, B) only or (A1 <: A, B) | (A, C1 <: C)
Further, a subclass of multiple edge type families could narrow the type of endpoints to any type that is a subtype of the type of endpoints of each of its direct edge type super families.

In order to prevent proliferation of feature codes, it seems acceptable to the author of this Language Opportunity to bundle this change with the existing feature, as the proposed relaxation of would allow more graph types to be valid and hence would not cause backwards compatibility issues.
In summary:

ulist.item: Consider adding the terminological concept of an edge type family for a group of edge types with the same key label set (as can be defined by supporting ).

Change to only require structural-endpoint consistency with implied ETS that are not part of an edge type family and with at least one implied ETS per direct super edge type family, for implementations that provide .

LO.brief: Extend LET with support for windowing

problem.para: GQL currently has no support for window functions, however, many of the required ingredients are beginning to be in place:

ulist.item: already proposes the introduction of partitioned procedure calls.
The is freely placeable, thus allowing us to enforce the in-order processing of the incoming binding table by a subsequent statement.

problem.para: What is missing is essentially framing (5 ROWS PRECEDING) and certain window-sensitive functions ( RANK).
As a possible approach, this LO proposes to extend the with support for framing over the incoming binding table as follows:

Evaluation semantics would treat all variables from the current working table as grouping variables containing the values in the window for the current row and corresponding column. This approach would enable re-use of horizontal aggregation functionality for the actual evaluation of aggregates in the window.
Caveats:

ulist.item: Due to the rewrites involved in the current specification in LET, realizing this approach will likely move the framing feature to variable definitions.
A full analysis of the windowing capabilities should be performed to ensure possibly feature parity of this approach.
Horizontal aggregation functionality needs to be expanded for this to become practical.
Window-sensitive expressions like RANK() need to be added, too.

problem.para: Currently, GQL provides no mechanism for explicitly replacing the current working table with a binding table provided by a catalog reference or an expression.
Available functionality to that end is:

ulist.item: FINISH, for establishing a unit binding table to start from.
CALL for unwinding the columns of the result of a procedure call (currently lacking table support).
FOR record_var IN table_expression, for iterating over the records of a table.

problem.para: Beyond these features, there appears to be a gap for just replacing the current working table. Possible approaches might be:

ulist.item: Extend named CALL to also iterate tables ( solve by FINISH and extending CALL).
Introduce dedicated syntax for replacing the current working table from a table expression ( solve by a new construct such as FROM table_expression).
Introduce dedicated syntax for replacing the current record from a record expression ( solve by FINISH, FOR record_var IN table_expression, and a new construct such as RETURN AS ROW).

problem.para: A feature for replacing the current working table with the result of a table expression should be added.

GQL has no dedicated statement for expressing full outer cross joins or full outer natural joins. While CALL can be used to that effect, the required linearization and syntactic duplication of subqueries is cumbersome at best.

Consider adding a new optional statement at the same level of set operations for performing cross joins, natural joins and their full outer counter parts to close a gap in relational capabilities of GQL.

ulist.item: { } [ NATURAL | CROSS ] JOIN { }
{ } OPTIONAL [ NATURAL | CROSS ] JOIN { }

problem.para: (NATURAL being the default)

A complimentary option would be to allow list behavior to be specified as a part of a or a .

The finer granularity for specifying list reference behavior is critical for supporting procedures stored in a GQL databases and for porting code segments between GQL implementations and porting code segments between GQL and SQL/PGQ.

Support for extensible key constraints, key constraints that allow subconstraint scopes to add additional key value components to an already effective key value component specification, should be considered.

LO.brief: Support for deferred and unenforced constraints

problem.para: SQL:

alist.item: Distinguishes between initially immediate or initially deferred constraints to control when constraint checking occurs initially.
Whether constraint checking may be deferred at all.
whether the constraint is currently enforced or not.

problem.para: Also, consider syntax for manually triggering constraint checking for an explicitly referenced graph or the current working graph, REQUIRE emp_pk or REQUIRE *).
Development of similar capabilities should be considered for GQL.
See also .

The current design for key constraints does not support weak entity key constraints, even though a design for weak entity key constraints is already available in PG-KEYS. This functionality is critical and should be added.
The following syntactic approaches could be considered for extending the current design with support for weak entity key constraints:

ulist.item:
Allow specifying the focus variable of a key constraint, like so:
FOR n IN (n:A)-[e:E]->(m:B)

Allow specifying separate scope and constraint patterns, like so:
FOR (a:A) WITHIN (a)-[e]->(b)
Both.

problem.para: The current design for key constraints specifies the semantics of constraint checking in terms of the result of certain queries, which are generated by the Syntax Rules of .

This could be challenging for providing mathematical proofs of key characteristics of the design and thus specifying the semantics of constrain checking more directly should be considered as a possible alternative.

The current design for key constraints requires key component values to be null-free. The precise details of null handling in key and unique constraints should be revisited in light of similar functionality in ISO/IEC 9075 SQL (unique with nulls distinct, unique with nulls not distinct).
See .
The current design for key constraints only support the specification of covariant constraint patterns. The addition of support for invariant constraint patterns should be considered.

Background: An invariant constraint pattern would be a constraint pattern that specifies the exact set of labels and properties required of matched nodes and edges. A covariant constraint pattern only specifies the minimally (at least) required labels and properties of matched nodes and edges.
The question of invariant pattern support naturally extends to the pattern matching language at large, as well as SQL/PGQ (at least for label expressions).

The current design for key constraints is specific to the handling of graph types and graphs in GQL. For compatibility, it should be demonstrated that this design is equivalent in expressive power to how node and edge identity is established in the tabular property graph model of SQL/PGQ. Any gaps discovered in this regard should be addressed.
See also .

The current design for integrity constraints allows implementations to defer constraint enforcement until the current transaction is committed. This allows a data-modifying operation to temporarily violate a constraint. In turn, it becomes impossible to trust whether a passed graph actually upholds the constraints of its graph type or not!
This topic requires further investigation. The following options could be explored to improve the current situation:

ulist.item: Introduction of explicit syntax for triggering constraint enforcement.
Tightening the rules of constraint enforcement, such as requiring constraint enforcement to happen at assignment time.

Introduction of additional annotations to constraint definitions for providing more precise control to the user regarding the timing of constraint enforcement and the guarantees offered by a graph of a given graph type.
Introduction of a facility for the deferred execution of data-modifying operations as a means for ensuring that such updates are immediately followed by constraint enforcement.
Introduction of explicit syntax for temporarily disabling constraint enforcement.

problem.para: Resolving this issue will very likely also require revisiting the rules that enforce the relationship between graphs and their graph types in order to avoid exceptions to be raised untimely due to delayed enforcement of constraints!
See also .

PP.brief: Syntax ambiguity in specifying constraint requirements

problem.para: The current syntax for the definition of integrity constraints places the constraint kind of a constraint requirement in tail position ( IS KEY). While feasible in principle, this is not a very extensible approach that might lead to difficulties regarding parsing when introducing new constraint kinds in the future, due to the tail positioning of the essential disambiguating syntax.
Alternative or at least additional syntax that allows specifiying the constraint kind in head position should be considered, such as:
problem.code: CONSTRAINT myConstraint FOR REQUIRE KEY(k1, k2)

problem.para: Support for attaching constraint definitions directly to element type definitions via additional syntax shorthands should be considered, such as:
problem.code: (:Person => :HasAddress { first :: STRING, last :: String => address :: STRING })

problem.para: Support for defining primary constraint aspect objects outside of graphs and/or graph types whose definition declaratively selects constraint subjects from the catalog should be considered.
This would allow defining constraints independently in a way that is not directly tied to their subjects or the types of their subjects and perhaps can be seen as a form of aspect-orientation.
Syntax sketch:
problem.code: CREATE CONSTRAINT myConstraint ON /mySchema/myDir1/myGraph FOR REQUIRE

problem.para: Support for defining general check constraints should be added.
Limiting the expressive power of supported checks needs to be considered.
Adding support for defining check constraints in terms of JSON-schema should be considered.
This likely requires the addition of various independent features:

ulist.item: Support for general check constraints. See .
Support for generating and parsing a well-defined JSON-representation of GQL values.

Addition of a new predicate for testing whether the JSON-representation of a given GQL value would adhere to a given JSON-schema. Defining this predicate requires to determine how JSON-schemas should be referenced within GQL.

One approach could be:

olist.item: Clearly distinguish horizontal from vertical aggregation depending on whether group list variables are referenced or not.
Rewrite horizontal aggregates to scalar value expressions that use vertical aggregates.
Focus expression semantics on vertical aggregates only.
